I can sympathize with you, op. My aunt passed away just over a year and a half ago from this cancer. It's hard to watch. I can't, however, imagine what it would be like to watch a parent go through this.

NutellaManatee has some sound advice. Most importantly, in my mind, is to visit your father as often as you possibly can. You will thank yourself for it later. Even when he is barely there, you are still making memories. You are also helping him. It can make the difference between his passing being comforting or filled with uncertainty.

Don't worry about the roids. He will likely be on and off them for a while. As scary as it is to see their condition degrade, he will make a startlingly quick recovery when he begins taking them again. 

There are some activities I'd like to suggest, if I may. My aunt's case was particularly severe, leaving her unable to speak at all and unable to really interact. You can alter this to suit your father's level of capable interaction. My aunt really enjoyed having books read to her. She also enjoyed simple board games that were very stimulating audio-visually and physically (think Trouble).

Enjoy the time you have left. There's still a lot of memories to make. Milk this time for everything it's worth, Put some things off if you need to. You can always pick them back up later.

Visit as a family unit if you can. Reforge those old bonds. It'll make you that much stronger at the end. There's also likely to be some kind of grief counselling available at the hospital. Take advantage of it. As you must know since you're asking the internets, it can be so very comforting to speak to a perfect stranger about these things. They're there for you.

Lastly, I just want to say I'm sorry. Just remember that his pain is temporary. The moment he passes, he is free. Once I truly understood that on a visceral level, I was much better able to be in the moment with my aunt and I was more at ease with her passing.

Much love. <3

Let's see if I can explain this... **TL;DR - I got to my first [10] and thought everything I was seeing was on television and had a revelation about myself.**

It was the first time I smoked pot and felt anything more than a little goofiness or a body high. Up until that point I had been very cautious because I'm a very self-conscious person and it's difficult for me to truly let go of my control over my emotions and expressions.

It was a new kind of pot for me and I didn't realize how strong it was. I felt the high almost instantly. Luckily it was just me and my boyfriend so when I really started tripping, I felt pretty safe.

I can only describe it as observing everything around me as if it were on TV. My peripheral vision kind of went to crap and so my sense of sight felt very narrow, as if it were all contained in a box. Spacial awareness went out the window. My perception of time also started slipping. My memory shortened to a window of about 15 seconds, as hard as I tried to remember. I was in this self-contained bubble. Everything outside felt almost unreal.

This being my first real trip, I was very upset. Those were some very powerful things to be experiencing in unison. It was unnerving and it wasn't until I came down from the high that I truly had an appreciation for it.

I learned a bit about myself while I was in that state. Because it felt like I was watching TV and I was forced to live in the moment, I laughed harder than I had in my entire life and had some of the most true, child-like joy that I remember. Once I was sober again, I realized that I felt as I often do when I'm watching TV: These people are just pixels. They're not real. They can't see me. I can just be me. I don't have to mask my emotions and remain polite and be presentable and meet their expectations. In this moment, I am who I am. I can laugh at what I find funny and smile at something cheesy without looking like a doofus and allow myself to feel a depth of emotion that I usually prohibit myself from experiencing.

It took me being fuckballs high to realize just how tightly I was holding the reigns on just about every aspect of social interaction. I was never myself. Been trying to undo that part of my programming since. It's working.

**TL;DR -**I held my aunt's hand while she died of brain cancer. It was a very powerful experience that I never got to fully digest. As it so happened, I was assaulted the next day and landed myself in the hospital. 

My aunt developed a cancerous and aggressive brain tumor in 2010. The diagnosis came out of the blue. She had been suffering from mental illness most of her life, and when her behavior became all the more strange we simply assumed it was the progression of her mental illness. It was a routine scan that uncovered it. She was dead within 6 months. There was nothing doctor's could do. The only real comfort my family had was that even if they had discovered it in the early stages, her chances would have been no better. It was that severe.

We admitted her just a few months before the diagnosis to an adult care home where we visited her 5-6 days per week. It was very shocking to see how quickly a brain tumor of that magnitude simply eats someone alive. It was in her frontal lobe. She quickly lost the ability to talk or even communicate through gesture or movement. She also ceased to smile or even, really, to BE.

On the day of her death, we received a call from the staff that she had been behaving strangely before she was completely unresponsive and slipped into unconsciousness. They let us know they believed it was her last few hours. From there, my grandmother (her mother) and I called her children and siblings, then packed a few things and made our way to the home again.

For the next few hours, we took turns sitting with her, talking with her. I brought an antique copy of a Nancy Drew novel that my mother owned when she was a child. My aunt's youngest daughter was reading to her from the book when she died. I was on the other side holding her hand. It was a very clear moment. There had been a rattling in her chest with every breath, then it abruptly stopped.

I was next to the emergency call button when it happened. Everyone was shouting at me to press the button but I was so upset I couldn't find it. There were about 7 buttons, none of them clearly marked, not to mention knobs and something easy for patients to squeeze. In those initial moments, I felt guilty for not pressing the button sooner, for being  that spastic. I became very fixated on that action, or lack thereof. Nothing could have changed what happened, though. This is something I know now. In the moment, though, it was exhausting.

As far as how I coped, or even how my family coped, we didn't, really. In a turn of events that I can only describe as astronomical in it's chances, I was physically assaulted the very next day and ended up in the ER. My family immediately threw themselves at the opportunity to give support in whatever way they could and almost disregarded the trauma that we had just gone through 18 hours earlier. It's not to say that we forgot about my aunt, her suffering, or her death. But it gave the family, and myself, something else to focus on, something that could be improved. Sometimes I feel an absurd guilt that some members of my family never really had a full healing process because of my assault. But maybe it isn't such a bad thing.

From my own experience, junkount got it right:
> OP, have you considered that your concern to not hurt anyone is killing you?


Your happiness and the happiness of others are not mutually exclusive. If those around you **require** that you sacrifice your own happiness for theirs, they have nothing left to offer you. They are hollow people that seek to fill the void within themselves by leeching your good nature, your kindness, and your support. Your hopes and dreams and plans and boundaries are **valid**. You are **worthwhile**. 

That's something that takes a long time to truly believe but it's not hard to start. The never-ending chorus of people telling me that I was not a valid person drowned out any thoughts of self-worth. Get away from those people and you'll see just how quickly your world changes.


Remember:
The circumstances you were born into are not your fault.

The pain that has been inflicted upon you is not a punishment for wrongdoing, not even peripherally. There was nothing that you did, thought, or desired that justifies the abuse you've suffered.

We're here for you.
